title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
extended_summary:
This report examines how a generative AI platform can be integrated into real secondary school classrooms as a teaching partner, rather than as a standalone tutoring or laboratory tool. The central question is how teachers design, frame, and supervise AI-supported activities so that AI adds instructional value while preserving human judgment, curricular alignment, and teacher authority.

The intervention was the Colleague AI Classroom pilot, a seven-week co-design study in which 21 in-service teachers from Washington State public school districts and one independent school used four AI features: Teaching Aide, AI-assisted Assessment and Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. More than 600 students in grades 6-12 participated in classroom activities designed and facilitated by their teachers. Teachers planned lessons, implemented AI-supported activities in live classrooms, and provided weekly reflections, interviews, surveys, planning forms, and usage logs that informed iterative tool refinement.

The study found that AI was most effective when teachers actively scaffolded its use, aligned it to instructional goals, and retained oversight over prompts, grading, and interpretation of feedback. Teachers valued the platform most for formative feedback, conversational support, and class-level insight generation, especially when AI outputs were short, clear, standards-aligned, and editable. The report concludes that generative AI can meaningfully extend classroom instruction as a "third agent" only when teachers remain central mediators, and it emphasizes the importance of teacher AI competency, developmentally appropriate design, and human oversight for trustworthy school-based implementation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / LLM-based classroom platform used for teacher-guided student conversations, rubric generation, automated formative feedback, AI tutoring, and student-growth analytics.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied through the Colleague AI Classroom pilot in real K-12 classrooms, where in-service teachers co-designed and implemented four features: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights.

findings.finding_summary: In a seven-week pilot with 21 in-service teachers across four Washington State public school districts and one independent school, teachers reported that the platform could support classroom instruction when teacher-framed and scaffolded. The report emphasizes that pedagogical judgment and AI competency jointly shaped implementation quality, with teachers using the system as a 'third agent' while retaining final authority.
findings.measure: Teacher surveys, planning/reflection forms, group meetings, one-on-one interviews, and platform usage logs; teacher-reported implementation quality and confidence

findings.finding_summary: For the Teaching Aide feature, 35% of teacher-reported implementations indicated the AI helped most students learn, 62% indicated some students learned from the tool, and 3% indicated no student benefit. Teachers said thoughtful engagement and learning were strongest when they provided clear framing, modeled prompts, and tied the AI activity to instructional goals.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated student learning from AI-assisted conversations

findings.finding_summary: For AI-assisted conversations, 28% of teacher-reported implementations had most students engage thoughtfully, 66% were mixed, and 6% showed limited engagement. Engagement improved with repeated use, strong teacher presence, explicit norms, and clear finish lines, but outcomes varied by grade band and subject.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated student engagement in Teaching Aide conversations

findings.finding_summary: In the assessment workflow, the system produced high automated-grading coverage: median AI grading coverage on submitted work was 92.2% across 58 classroom-level assessment records, with a mean submission rate of 54.8% and an average resubmission rate of 8.7%. Teachers used the tool mainly for in-class formative assessments and revision cycles.
findings.measure: Platform usage logs for assessment grading and resubmissions

findings.finding_summary: Teachers found the AI-generated rubrics moderately useful: 60% indicated the rubrics could be used in classroom assignments with minor revisions, while 12% did not use AI-generated rubrics, 4% said they needed major revisions, 3% said the rubrics covered all key criteria, and 7% said the rubrics could not be applied. Teachers valued the generated feedback more than the numeric scores, but many reported score inconsistency and misalignment with their rubrics.
findings.measure: Teacher survey responses on rubric usefulness and assessment feedback quality
findings.sample_size: n=13 teacher survey responses on assessment feedback; n=19 teachers used assessments

findings.finding_summary: On assessment feedback quality, 57% of teachers said the AI provided clear, actionable feedback for teachers or students; 41% said it was useful for both teachers and students, 14% for students only, and 3% for teachers only. At the same time, 42% said the feedback was not useful, including 24% who found it vague or unhelpful and 18% who found it incorrect or misleading.
findings.measure: Teacher survey responses on AI-generated feedback usefulness

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods pilot and implementation report rather than a controlled efficacy study. It provides rich real-world evidence, but outcomes are mostly teacher-reported and descriptive, with no causal design or formal effect estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The report suggests practical instructional value, especially for formative feedback and teacher workflow support, but it does not report effect sizes or directly measured student outcome gains. Impact is promising yet unclear in magnitude.
